# Application of Non-Linear Principal Component Analysis to Hyperspectral data for noise filtering using artificial neural networks

##### Piscini, A.; Licciardi, G.

* * *

#### Workshop on Hyperspectral Image and Signal Processing, Evolution in Remote Sensing 2014-June: 8077576

#### 2014

* * *

ISSN/ISBN: 2158-6276

DOI: 10.1109/whispers.2014.8077576
Accession: 106025669

##### Summary

This work describes results of noise filtering techniques based on a Non-Linear Principal Component Analysis (NLPCA), applied to Hyperspectral CASI remote sensed data. NLPCA was carried out using Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) which are capable of modeling data non-linearity. NLPCA operated feature extraction on which original data were reconstructed, filtering the noise which affects first VNIR bands. Such a technique cleans VNIR bands, but does not affect the signal of other bands (SWIR). In order to appreciate improvements in classification due to noise filtering a supervised classification algorithm, based on Support Vector Machines (SVM), was applied to both original, noise filtered data, and NLPCA components (NLPCs). Results show that classification obtained using NLPCA-derived data is more accurate. Finally, SVM classification was also applied to fused images adding LiDAR Digital Surface Model (DSM) to the NLPCs and the original image in order to evaluate further improvements introduced by the dimensionality reduction offered by the NLPCA. Results show that the proposed method is able to improve the classification both by reducing dimensionality and suppressing the noise.

Session FRI-P-A : Noise Reduction                                                                 78

HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE NOISE REDUCTION AND ITS EFFECT ON SPECTRAL UNMIXING

Azam Karami, iMinds- Visionlab, University of Antwerp, Belgium  
Department of Electrical Engineering, Shahid Bahonar University of Kerman, Kerman, Iran  
Rob Heylen and Paul Scheunders, iMinds- Visionlab, University of Antwerp, Belgium

**Abstract :** In hyperspectral images (HSI), many of the spectral bands have low noise levels (LN bands) while some have high noise levels (junk bands). If a noise reduction algorithm is globally applied to the whole dataset, it usually affects the LN bands adversely. Therefore, we consider different criteria for denoising LN and junk bands. First, we discriminate between LN and junk bands using the spectral correlation between adjacent bands. After that, the mirror- extended curvelet transform is applied to all spectral bands. Next, each LN band is denoised using a soft thresholding technique, while a local noise reduction method is used for the junk bands, where the curvelet coefficients of adjacent LN bands are used to recover the junk bands. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Abstract. A new algorithm is described for estimating the noise model

parameters in hyperspectral data when neither noise components var-

iance nor noise spatial/spectral correlation priors are available. A maxi-

mum likelihood (ML) technique is introduced for checking the noise

spatial correlation hypothesis and estimating the spatial correlation func-

tion width alongside with estimating signal-independent and signal-depen-

dent noise components variance. The hyperspectral image is assumed to

match a limited set of assumptions. A three-dimensional (3-D) fractional

Brownian motion (fBm) model is introduced for describing locally the tex-

ture of the 3-D image noisy textural fragment. Nonstationarity of the useful

image signal is taken into account by performing the estimation locally on a

3-D block-by-block basis. The accuracy of the proposed algorithm is first

illustrated for synthetic images obtained from either pure fBm or almost

noise-free AVIRIS hyperspectral images artificially degraded with spatially

correlated noise. The results obtained for synthetic images demonstrate

appropriate accuracy and robustness of the proposed method. Then

results obtained for real life AVIRIS hyperspectral data sets confirm the

noise spatial uncorrelation hypothesis for images acquired by the AVIRIS

sensor. Conclusions and open problems are outlined. ©2012 Society of Photo-

Optical Instrumentation Engineers (SPIE). [DOI: 10.1117/1.OE.51.11.111712]

Subject terms: hyperspectral imagery; fractal Brownian motion; noise modeling;

noise estimation; signal-dependent noise; noise covariance matrix.

There is no clear evidences in the literature corroborating

or rejecting the noise spectrally/spatially correlation hypoth-

esis for hyperspectral data.7,8,17,18 Note that most methods for

processing hyperspectral data mostly simplify the evaluation

by regarding the noise as a zero-mean white Gaussian noise

independent of the useful signal, i.e., noise is assumed

spatially and spectrally uncorrelated (with a diagonal noise

covariance matrix). They overcome the complexity with

assumptions that might be unrealistic as noise can be some-

what correlated along and across track by slightly differ-

ent extents,13 both spatially and spectrally depending on

operational conditions at acquisition time.

In practice, the noise three-dimensional (2-D) correlation

function or spectrum can be jointly estimated with the noise

standard deviation (STD) directly from each spectral band

of a noisy hyperspectral image. While for a few images it

is sometimes possible to carry out manual (interactive)

image analysis for the determination of the noise 2-D corre-

lation function for manually selected image fragments, it

becomes impossible or too labor-consuming to perform

such actions for hyperspectral data, especially if estimation

is to be done on-board or under conditions of fast acquisi-

tion and processing of images. Then it is better to apply

blind or automatic estimation methods,5 namely for detecting

homogeneous areas better suited to this task, as they allow

avoiding subjectivity and heterogeneity of manually selected

image fragments, even carefully selected. In Ref. 19, noise

correlation estimation is performed by analyzing the

observed data in blocks of fixed size in discrete cosine

transform (DCT) domain.

Some recent methods for estimating the noise parameters

take into account the possible spatial and/or spectral correla-


CCD sensors,23,24 or for hyperspectral sensors.25

In this paper, unlike recent methods which rely on the

assumptions of either spectrally and/or spatially correlated

SI noise, or spectrally and spatially uncorrelated mixture

of SI and signal-dependent noise components, a more com-

plex model is used. The noise is assumed to be a mixture of

SI and signal-dependent (Poisson-like) components, with

unknown variance and exhibiting at least spatial correlation

in both spatial dimensions (along and across track). How-

ever, we also assume spatial invariance of noise spatial

spectrum.

The new fully automatic technique we propose, denoted

vcNI þ fBm (“v”for vector, “c”for correlated, “NI”for

noise informative (NI) and “fBm”for fractal Brownian

motion model), infers noise model parameters directly

from the acquired data, with limited assumptions on noise

and useful signal, as mentioned above. We carry out ML esti-

mation based on a three-dimensional (3-D) fBm model for

describing locally the texture of the 3-D noisy image textural

multicomponent scanning window (MSW). The useful

signal is assumed to be strongly correlated in the spectral

direction while conversely the noise is considered spectrally

uncorrelated (lonely remaining assumption on noise). The

algorithm then estimates the covariance matrix or, more

exactly, its main lobe width for the spatially correlated

noise, and we account for the nonstationarity of the useful

image signal by performing the estimation locally on a

3-D block-by-block basis and at the pixel level.

By using maximum relative Cramer-Rao lower bound

(CRLB) on noise STD/variance among all bands involved

in a MSW, it becomes possible to first detect those

MSWs in an hyperspectral image that provide a required esti-

mation accuracy. These reliable MSWs are then selected for

defining a set of NI MSWs in the hyperspectral image. This

specific set is later used for estimating the final SI þ SD

Note, however, that our scheme can be extended to handle

spectrally correlated noise case as well, and that weak inter-

band spectral correlation has been shown to have negligible

impact on estimation accuracy for spatial correlation coeffi-

cients. But it has larger influence on accuracy of obtained

SI, SD variance estimates for pure fBm data degraded

synthetically.

In order to assess its intrinsic efficiency, this new method

is successively applied to pure fBm data and hyperspectral

data, both degraded with a mixture of SI and SD noise

components, spatially correlated. Then, results obtained

for real AVIRIS data are reported and discussed. The remain-

der part of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. 2, the

vNI þ fBm estimator is briefly recalled and its extension to

the spatially correlated noise case is introduced and detailed.

In Sec. 3, the properties of the new algorithm are assessed

both on simulated and real data degraded synthetically with

spatially correlated noise. In Sec. 4, results obtained for real

life AVIRIS data are reported and discussed, before conclud-

ing and highlighting perspectives.

2 Joint Estimation of Band Noise Variance and

Spatial Correlation Function Width

In a recent work of the authors,20 the problem of blind esti-

mation of noise affecting multicomponent or hyperspectral

images has been considered under noise spatially/spectrally

uncorrelatedness hypothesis. Both SI and signal-dependent

band noise components have been assumed. A distinctive

feature of this estimator is that texture parameters (rough-

ness, amplitude, inter-band correlation) and noise parameters

(variance, correlation function width) estimation tasks are

viewed as interdependent and solved jointly. The estimator

operates on 3-D image noisy textural fragment or MSW (for

example, 11 ×11 pixels in 7 adjacent bands) basis and ben-

efits from both spatial and spectral domains to effectively

decorrelate image texture and noise. We have shown that

good accuracy of band noise STD estimation can be

reached by using only a single MSW for a significant

percentage of hyperspectral image MSWs (10% to 50%).

For a single MSW we assume pure additive noise model.

Later, by aggregating together noise STD estimates from

many MSWs with different intensities, it becomes possible

to estimate SI and SD noise components variance. This is

done by applying a linear fit (nonrobust) in intensity-

variance plane. Experiments on the well-known AVIRIS

sensor have shown the proposed estimator accuracy to be

comparable to estimates obtained from the sensor calibration

data.

Now, to decide is noise spatially correlated or not, one

needs a technique for estimating noise spatial correlation

function or its parameter(s) for an image at hand indepen-

dently or jointly with other parameters of the noise. Here,

as a step forward, we would like to relax the first hypothesis

of spatial uncorrelatedness. This is done by introducing noise

spatial correlation matrix with unknown spatial correlation

function width. This width is to be estimated on MSWs

basis jointly with texture parameters and band noise STD.

the method is to be tested for data with known properties

4 Conclusions

In this paper, an extension of the previous hyperspectral

images noise variance estimator to spatially correlated

noise case has been proposed. The proposed approach is

able to jointly estimate the band noise (SI) additive and

SD components variance alongside with the noise spatial

correlation function width. Exponential correlation function

model has been considered at the current stage but other

models could be employed within the same framework.

The validity of the vcNI þ fBm has been shown through the

number of experiments including noise parameters estimation

# Estimation of correlated noise in hyperspectral images

##### Mahmood, A.; Robin, A.; Sears, M.

* * *

#### Workshop on Hyperspectral Image and Signal Processing, Evolution in Remote Sensing 2014-June: 8077550

#### 2014

* * *

ISSN/ISBN: 2158-6276

DOI: 10.1109/whispers.2014.8077550
Accession: 106025684


##### Summary

Many hyperspectral image processing algorithms (e.g detection, classification, endmember extraction etc.) are generally designed with the assumption of no spectral or spatial correlation in noise. However, studies [1, 2] have shown the presence of non-negligible correlation between the noise samples in different spectral bands, especially between noise of adjacent bands. It was also shown recently [3] that many well-known endmember extraction algorithms e.g. [4] give poor estimates for the number of endmembers in the presence of correlated noise. This asks for a precise estimation of noise for cases where noise is spectrally correlated. We show in this paper that the commonly employed hyperspectral noise estimation algorithm based on regression residuals [5, 6, 4] is very affected by spectrally correlated noise and we suggest a modified approach that proves to be very robust to noise correlation. Simulation results show that the estimation error is reduced at times by a factor of 5 when there is high spectral correlation in the noise.

HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE NOISE REDUCTION AND ITS EFFECT ON SPECTRAL UNMIXING

Azam Karami, iMinds- Visionlab, University of Antwerp, Belgium  
Department of Electrical Engineering, Shahid Bahonar University of Kerman, Kerman, Iran  
Rob Heylen and Paul Scheunders, iMinds- Visionlab, University of Antwerp, Belgium

**Abstract :** In hyperspectral images (HSI), many of the spectral bands have low noise levels (LN bands) while some have high noise levels (junk bands). If a noise reduction algorithm is globally applied to the whole dataset, it usually affects the LN bands adversely. Therefore, we consider different criteria for denoising LN and junk bands. First, we discriminate between LN and junk bands using the spectral correlation between adjacent bands. After that, the mirror- extended curvelet transform is applied to all spectral bands. Next, each LN band is denoised using a soft thresholding technique, while a local noise reduction method is used for the junk bands, where the curvelet coefficients of adjacent LN bands are used to recover the junk bands. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Abstract

:

Hyperspectral remote sensing is based on measuring the scattered and reflected electromagnetic signals from the Earth’s surface emitted by the Sun. The received radiance at the sensor is usually degraded by atmospheric effects and instrumental (sensor) noises which include thermal (Johnson) noise, quantization noise, and shot (photon) noise. Noise reduction is often considered as a preprocessing step for hyperspectral imagery. In the past decade, hyperspectral noise reduction techniques have evolved substantially from two dimensional bandwise techniques to three dimensional ones, and varieties of low-rank methods have been forwarded to improve the signal to noise ratio of the observed data. Despite all the developments and advances, there is a lack of a comprehensive overview of these techniques and their impact on hyperspectral imagery applications. In this paper, we address the following two main issues; (1) Providing an overview of the techniques developed in the past decade for hyperspectral image noise reduction; (2) Discussing the performance of these techniques by applying them as a preprocessing step to improve a hyperspectral image analysis task, i.e., classification. Additionally, this paper discusses about the hyperspectral image modeling and denoising challenges. Furthermore, different noise types that exist in hyperspectral images have been described. The denoising experiments have confirmed the advantages of the use of low-rank denoising techniques compared to the other denoising techniques in terms of signal to noise ratio and spectral angle distance. In the classification experiments, classification accuracies have improved when denoising techniques have been applied as a preprocessing step.
